3.4 Association between changes in functional connectivity and letter accuracy

description.value: The study examined whether anodal tDCS over the left inferior frontal gyrus, delivered with speech-language therapy, changed resting-state functional connectivity and whether connectivity changes were associated with improvements in written naming in people with primary progressive aphasia.

spans.text: In the present study, we examined changes in functional connectivity in the language network, as identified in task-based fMRI studies of spoken and written word production, to determine whether functional connectivity change is a mechanism for tDCS effects in PPA.

design.value: This was a double-blinded, randomized, first-phase, between-subject comparison within a larger within-subject crossover trial, comparing participants initially assigned to tDCS versus sham, with both conditions paired with speech-language therapy.

spans.text: Participants belonged to a larger cohort who received tDCS and sham (plus language therapy) in a double-blinded, within-subject crossover design (see Clinical Trial Identifier: NCT02606422 on clinicaltrials.gov ).
we focus on data only from the first phase of stimulation in a between-subject design.
Half the patients in the present study were randomly assigned to the sham condition and half to tDCS.

The proxy we used to measure performance in written naming was letter accuracy instead of whole-word accuracy because we wanted to capture more subtle changes at the graphemic level as well as the letter-sound correspondences, i.e., to capture changes in both the lexical and sublexical representation of each word.

description.value: Percentage of letters corresponding to sounds making up words; each correct letter received one point and points were subtracted for deletions, additions, substitutions, transpositions, or movements.

spans.text: language treatment test scores (letter accuracy, i.e., percentage of letters corresponding to sounds making up words) were collected before and after the written naming/spelling treatment intervention, with percentage of correct letters as the primary outcome.

Spelling was scored on a rule-based system, in which each letter was given one point if correct, and points were subtracted if letters were deleted, added, substituted, transposed, or moved (see scoring system from Goodman and Caramazza, 1985 ).

The primary outcomes for the present study were changes in written naming because writing has the potential to be a good compensatory mechanism for alternative communication in cases of oral language decline in some PPA variants, as exemplified in the introduction.

2.3 Written word production/spelling intervention

task_description.value: Participants practiced oral and written picture naming and spelling using a spell-study-spell procedure, with trained and untrained word sets.

spans.text: The language therapy involved oral and written picture naming/spelling therapy, and was based on previously successful treatments of PPA patients by Beeson and Egnor following a spell-study-spell procedure in similar studies

design_type.value: between-subject first phase of a within-subject crossover design

spans.text: we focus on data only from the first phase of stimulation in a between-subject design.

instructions.value: The patient was shown a picture, asked to orally name the object, and then write it down; semantic cues and correct-word models were provided when necessary.

spans.text: each training trial, the patient was shown a picture on the computer, asked to orally name the object, and then write it down.

stimuli.value: Pictures of objects and trained word sets of 10–30 words.

spans.text: Each participant was trained in a set of 10–30 words according to the level of language severity
